To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
fathers show increased activation in brain regions associated with threat processing when they view an infant in danger, and this is related to protective behaviors in daily life.

the brain areas involved in paternal protection overlap with those involved in maternal protection, but that there is a unique pattern of activation in the motor areas for own (vs other) infants in threatening situations, and in the frontal pole for protective behavior in fathers.

fathers showed increased activation in the amygdaloid complex and the frontal pole when viewing threatening vs neutral situations with their own vs unknown infant, and that this activation was associated with fathers’ protective behavior in daily-life.

the development of protective behavior and the neural mechanisms underlying the perception of threat to infants
paternal protection and the underlying brain mechanisms.
the development of paternal responses to infants in danger, and the neural correlates of this behavior.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
fathers are more sensitive to infant-threatening vs neutral stimuli and show a stronger neural response to threat for their own vs an infant who is not their own.
the amygdala is activated in response to infant-threatening vs neutral stimuli and that this activation is stronger for own than unknown infants.
this study is the first one that describes neural mechanisms involved in the perception of danger to infants.

the brain areas involved in paternal protection are very similar to those involved in maternal protection and the differences are mainly quantitative.
